title: Scientists Trapped an Antimatter Particle for Months to Study Its Secrets
gist: A Northwestern team led by Gerald Gabrielse used a single-positron quantum cyclotron to hold one positron near absolute zero for months. Because the method does not destroy the particle, they could repeat quantum-state measurements. The result was published in Physical Review Letters, and the American Physical Society says the device could enable positron magnetic measurements about 30 times more precise than before. So far it has found no electron-positron difference.

insights.claim: Northwestern physicists led by Gerald Gabrielse built a single-positron quantum cyclotron. It uses electric and magnetic fields to hold one positron in a vacuum near absolute zero, its lowest energy state, so researchers can induce controlled quantum-state changes. The result was published in Physical Review Letters.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Precision particle trapping and control near absolute zero is an enabling technique that overlaps with quantum-device engineering.

insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Being able to measure the same particle again and again is what makes the large precision gains possible.

insights.claim: Studying antimatter is hard because antiparticles annihilate on contact with ordinary matter. Labs therefore isolate them in vacuum chambers with electromagnetic fields, which only partly solves the problem for quantum-scale experiments.

insights.claim: According to the American Physical Society, the new device could enable magnetic measurements of antimatter particles about 30 times more precise than before. Physicists want to compare positron and electron magnetic properties to look for small differences that could help explain why the universe is dominated by matter.
